newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumo star, HIV patient seek seats in Japan polls.
newsitem.headline: Sumo star, HIV patient seek seats in Japan polls.

text.p: A sumo wrestler, former tennis amd boxing stars, and Japan's first declared HIV-positive candidate are among those being put forward by parties seeking to attract apathetic voters in Sunday's election.

In a race in which all sides have taken the same platform on the main issue of streamlining government, the parties turned to celebrities and unusual candidates in key districts to draw an electorate expected to shun polls in record numbers.
Mainstream parties hope to repeat the success of two television comedians, who campaigned as independents and captured the governorships of Tokyo and Osaka last year.

Popular sumo wrestler Kyokudozan, 31, the first ever active practitioner of Japan's traditional national sport to compete for a parliamentary seat, has drawn crowds by dressing in an elaborate kimono with his hair in an oiled topknot.

"I'll do my utmost to change Japan," said Kyokudozan, whose real name is Kazuyasu Hata. He is campaigning on the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) list in the region around the western city of Osaka.

Shinshinto, shown in opinion polls to be trailing its conservative rival, the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), in the contest for the 500 seats in the Lower House of parliament, has seven celebrity candidates on its list.

Sachiyo Nomura, a television personality and wife of Katsuya Nomura, manager of professional baseball team Yakult Swallows, joined the Shinshinto ticket in a close-fought Tokyo district at the personal entreaty of party head Ichiro Ozawa.
The 64-year-old Nomura, a sharp-tongued commentator on television, has been vague about her platform, saying only that she wants to stress the "importance of being a good mother".
Shinshinto is also backing former professional tennis player Naoko Sato, 41, who retired in 1990 after 17 losing appearances at Wimbledon to become a television commentator.

The LDP, the strongest of the three parties in the previous ruling coalition, is running four celebrities. It has turned to former World Boxing Council lightweight champion Yuji "Guts" Ishimatsu in another tight Tokyo race.
The 47-year-old former boxer, who after retirement turned to acting, says he wants to improve education.
Political analyst Takayoshi Miyagawa of the Centre for Political Public Relations said celebrity candidates were not likely to fare well in Sunday's elections.
"Those who have gone straight from their previous careers without public service achievement will likely find fame is not enough to carry them with sceptical voters," he said.
Stressing policy over popularity, the newly formed Democratic Party is running the first candidate in Japan to publicly declare himself HIV-positive, a 36-year-old haemophiliac.
The candidate, Satoru Ienishi, contracted the virus which causes AIDS from unheated blood products.

Democratic Party co-leader Naoto Kan, the heath minister in the previous coalition, won widespread praise earlier this year for exposing his ministry's complicity in a scandal in which nearly 2,000 haemophiliacs were exposed to the HIV virus through tainted blood products.
"I want to improve the government system based on my experience as a HIV patient," Ienishi said while campaigning in his district of Nara, a historic capital in western Japan.
"I also want to encourage those suffering from HIV and in despair not to throw their dreams away."
